title: when I do and when I've done; if and when
subtitle: when I do / when I've done; if and when
summary: After when, while, before, after, until, as soon as and if, use a present tense (not will) to talk about the future.

lesson.heading: when I do (not when I will do)
lesson.text: Amy is on a train. She's calling a friend: '**I'll call** you again later **when I arrive**.' The sentence has two parts: the main part (I'll call you again later) and the when-part (when I arrive). The time is future ('later'), but Amy says *when I arrive*, not ~~when I will arrive~~. We say **when I do something** (not will do) and **when something happens** (not will happen).

examples.text: We'll go out **when it stops** raining.
**When you are** here again, you must come and see us.
Don't forget to lock the door **when you go** out.

lesson.heading: The same after while / before / after / as soon as / until
lesson.text: These time words work like when: the verb after them is present, even though the time is future.

examples.text: What are you going to do **while I'm away**?
**Before you go**, there's something I want to ask you.
Wait here **until I come back**. or ... **till I come back**.

lesson.heading: when I've done: one thing complete before the other
lesson.text: You can also use the present perfect (have done) after when / after / until / as soon as. We use it to show that one thing is complete *before* the other - the two things do not happen together. Do not use the present perfect if the two things happen together.

examples.text: Can I have the newspaper **when you've finished** with it?
Don't say anything while Ian is here. Wait **until he has gone**.
**When I've phoned** Kate, we can go out. (= first I'll phone Kate and after that we can go out)
**When I phone** Kate, I'll ask her about the party.

left.label: Present simple
examples: I'll come as soon as **I finish**.
You'll feel better after **you have** something to eat.

right.label: Present perfect
examples: I'll come as soon as **I've finished**.
You'll feel better after **you've had** something to eat.

lesson.heading: if + present for the future
lesson.text: After **if**, we normally use the present (if I do / if I see etc.) for the future.

examples.text: I'll be angry **if it happens** again.
Hurry up! **If we don't hurry**, we'll be late.

left.label: if = possibly
left.text: For things that will possibly happen (or not happen).
examples: **If it is raining** this evening, I won't go out. (not when it is raining)
Don't worry **if I'm late** tonight. (not when I'm late)
**If they don't come** soon, I'm not going to wait for them.
I might go out later. (it's possible) **If I go out**, I'll get some bread.

right.label: when = for sure
right.text: For things which are sure to happen.
examples: I'm going out later. (for sure) **When I go out**, I'll get some bread.

lesson.text: Will belongs in the main part of the sentence only. After when, while, before, after, until, as soon as and if, switch to the present.

exercises.prompt: As soon as we get any more information, ___ you know.
exercises.explanation: The main part of the sentence takes will; the present (we get) is only after as soon as.

exercises.prompt: I want to see Sophie before ___ away next week.
exercises.explanation: After before we use the present, even for next week: before she goes away.

exercises.statement: We'll go out when it will stop raining.
exercises.explanation: We'll go out when it stops raining. No will after when.

exercises.prompt: Remind your flatmate about the door before they leave.
exercises.answer: Don't forget to lock the door when you go out.
exercises.explanation: Present simple (you go out) after when, even though the time is future.

exercises.prompt: Don't drive through a red light. Wait until it ___ to green.
exercises.explanation: After until we use the present: until it changes.

exercises.prompt: I'm going out for about an hour. ___ here when I get back?
exercises.explanation: The main part is a will-question (Will you still be ...?); the present (I get) is after when.

exercises.prompt: Which word completes each sentence: if or when?

items.text: Be careful. You'll hurt yourself ... you fall.
I'm going away for a few days. I'll call you ... I get back.
I'm going shopping. ... you want anything, I can get it for you.
I'm watching a programme on TV right now. ... it finishes, I'm going to bed.
... I don't see you tomorrow, when will I see you again?
We can eat at home or, ... you prefer, we can go to a restaurant.
I hope Sarah can come to the party. It will be a shame ... she can't come.

exercises.prompt: You'll feel better after ___ something to eat.
exercises.explanation: After after we can use the present perfect (you've had) or present simple (you have), but never will.

exercises.prompt: Someone you know has been very rude to you, and you want her to apologise. You say: I won't speak to her until ___.
exercises.explanation: After until: present simple or present perfect, both are possible here.

exercises.statement: When I've phoned Kate, I'll ask her about the party.
exercises.explanation: When I phone Kate, I'll ask her about the party. Phoning and asking happen together, so the present perfect is wrong here.

exercises.prompt: I think everything will be fine, but if ___ any problems, I'll let you know, OK?
exercises.explanation: After if we use the present for the future: if there are any problems.

exercises.prompt: I might go out later. ___ I go out, I'll get some bread.
exercises.explanation: Going out is only possible, not certain, so if (not when).
